text.p: The U.S. unit of Teva Pharmaceuticals Industries Ltd said Tuesday it had suspended sales of antibiotic Clindamycin because of a warning letter from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration about manufacturing issues.

Nasdaq trading of the company's shares was halted Tuesday at 1315 EDT (1715 GMT) following a news report about the FDA warning letter, issued July 28, 1997, which led to a recall of five batches of the drug the same month.

Fletcher, whose parent company is Israel's largest pharmaceuticals business, said the manufacturing problem was limited to Clindamycin and had no bearing on about 30 other products Teva produces in the United States.

Earlier Tuesday, a company spokesman described the problem as "an isolated incident." Fletcher said it stemmed from Teva's recent switch to another supplier of the powdered active ingredient of Clindamycin.
"The previous supplier was from Italy, the new one is from China," he said, adding the FDA felt the company had not adequately tested new batches of the raw material.
Fletcher told Reuters that Teva will have to do "a whole bunch of testing on the material," before reintroducing the drug.

"There was no health hazard, but they have to make sure it (Clindamycin) is meeting all our criteria," FDA spokeswoman Susan Cruzan said. The criteria, she noted, are designed to ensure purity and stability of drug components.

David Saks, a Gruntal & Co pharmaceuticals analyst, said Teva told analysts earlier this month about the recall during a conference call about second quarter 1997 earnings. "It was a minor event that has no spillover effect," he said.
